text: The grandmother stays in the village, the mother stays in the county seat, and the girl leaves for the city on her own. Eighty-three minutes is not much room for three lives, and Wang Er Zhuo spends the brevity rather than apologising for it: each woman gets a stretch of ordinary time, and the cuts between them do the arithmetic. What sixty years of work asks of a body, what a county town does to a woman drowning in the middle of her life, what a city offers someone who arrives with nothing arranged — the three pressures are set side by side and weighted the same. The youngest is the only one still in motion, and the film declines to call that a promise. It is a position on a map the two women behind her have already crossed.

Moju is old, he fishes for a living, and he has announced that he will fight Dopor, the boli champion. Boli is Bangladeshi wrestling, a village sport with a titleholder everyone in the district can name, so the challenge is public from the second it is made and cannot be quietly withdrawn. Iqbal Hossain Chowdhury takes ninety-two minutes over it, and files the result under mystery and thriller as much as drama, which is the most useful thing to know going in: whatever is being settled here is not settled by the strength of an old man's arms. Ageing bodies in cinema are usually either comic or elegiac. This one is neither. It belongs to a man with a reason he does not explain, in a place small enough that everybody will be watching, and where the watching is half the point.

Thirteen minutes is the whole of it: an Eastern Orthodox parish in Concord, New Hampshire, working its way toward Pascha. Fay Efrosini Lellios is after the approach rather than the feast — the preparation that decides what the day will mean to the people who have done the preparing. Short nonfiction about worship has to choose between explaining a rite to outsiders and recording it for the ones who already keep it, and at this length there is no room for both. So the runtime becomes the argument. What fits inside it is faces, hands, repetition, the particular sound a small congregation makes, and the outline of a year organised around a date the surrounding calendar does not share. Nothing here is scaled up into a statement about faith in America. This parish, this town, this passage through it.

A summer in Spain, two friends, one painter — and an ex-wife who has not arrived yet. Woody Allen gives that setup ninety-six minutes and the mildest conditions available: a warm country, a holiday, nobody obliged to be anywhere. Whatever pressure exists has to come from the arrangement itself, which is why the balance of the film shifts when the ex-wife re-enters; an Academy Award for supporting actress came out of the picture, and the structure explains how a part arriving that late could carry that much. Two appetites are on trial — one that wants to be certain before it commits, one that commits in order to find out — and a summer abroad is exactly the container in which both can be tried and neither answered. The two visitors treat the country as a season. The people they meet are living in it, and the film notices the difference.

Joan Wilder writes passionate romance for a living and has no life of her own. Then a package arrives, her sister is being held for ransom, and she is on a plane to South America carrying the price — after which she takes the wrong bus and is set down in the jungle with a deadline and no idea where she is. The Academy Award this picture took was for editing, which is the honest prize for it: a kidnapping, a jungle crossing and a courtship all have to run at the same speed, and none of them may be allowed to stall the others. Robert Zemeckis is unusually patient about competence — what Joan can actually do gets established slowly, and it is not what she can imagine. A woman who has written a hundred versions of this is now inside one, on foot, with nothing she can revise.

Talent is the least of it: what the pop charts of the early 1960s ask of a soul trio is a set of adjustments made by other people. Bill Condon's film is about that process — the packaging, the personnel decisions, the rooms where singers are discussed rather than present — and it treats the record business as its subject rather than a backdrop for numbers. Two hours and ten minutes is room enough for careers rather than a season, which changes what the songs are for: each one lands at a different stage of a bargain. The Academy Award it took for sound reads like a technician's footnote and sits closer to the centre, since the story is about a sound being smoothed until a larger audience will buy it. Crossing over is achieved here. The film keeps the invoice in view, and every line of it is signed for by someone in the group.

The idea is hers, the name attached to it is her boss's, and so she borrows the name. Mike Nichols builds the rest from the details that decide who gets heard inside a corporation: a borrowed suit, a phone manner, which door a person comes in by, whether a room assumes competence follows from the desk someone happens to sit at. The comedy is exact about the mechanics of the fraud, where a meeting can be lost on one wrong word, and unsentimental about why the fraud is necessary at all: the 1988 office is arranged so that the person with the idea and the person permitted to present it are never the same person. There is a romance, kept firmly second to the deal. The tension is not whether she is capable. It is how long capability can be run under someone else's signature.

Two long-range guns on a Nazi-held island cover the water, and two thousand British soldiers are stuck on the wrong side of them. The job is to get in and destroy the guns. J. Lee Thompson takes two hours and forty minutes over that one sentence, which locates his interest exactly: not the demolition but the approach — the crossing, the weather, the waiting, the days of small decisions made by tired men who disagree about what they are prepared to do to each other to finish. Every man on the team is a specialist, so each is indispensable in one respect and a liability in all the others, and the film is patient enough to let that arithmetic run. Made in 1961, close enough to the war that a good part of its audience had been in it, the picture keeps its heroism conditional and its cost itemised.

Frankenstein wants out of the business, and a former teacher arrives to inform him that he is not finished. The second creature gets built under something close to blackmail, which is the real shift this sequel makes: the first time, a man overreached on his own; here he is pressed back into the work by someone with steadier nerves and less to lose. James Whale had seventy-five minutes and a studio expecting a horror picture. He delivered one, and ran a comedy through it at a pitch where menace and absurdity are not separable, so that no reaction is ever confirmed as the right one. The monster survived a mob and is now party to a bargain nobody consulted him about. Whatever else it is doing, the film never lets the creature be only an effect, and it insists on that from the first reel to the last.

Every daughter who falls in love takes another piece out of the arrangement her father was raised inside. He delivers milk, he is poor, and the village he lives in runs on rules he could recite in his sleep, until reciting them stops being enough. Norman Jewison uses three hours for something a shorter film could not buy: enough time inside the village that its customs feel like architecture before they start coming apart. Two clocks run at once. In the house, love keeps arriving in the wrong order and asking for a blessing anyway. Outside it, in a Russia that has not had its revolution yet, antisemitism is tightening, and every concession the father makes at home is made on ground that is being taken out from under him. Poverty here is not decor but arithmetic: what a dowry costs, what a match without one costs, what it costs to say no.

Brontë Mitchell wants an apartment the building will only rent to a married couple; Georges Fauré wants to stay in the country. The contract they sign is meant to be filed and forgotten, and then the immigration service takes an interest, and two strangers have to assemble a shared past that will survive questioning. Peter Weir plays this as pressure rather than farce: every rehearsal of the invented history is a real conversation neither of them would have started, and neither can walk away, because the apartment and the visa are as concrete as rent. Registered as a French production, shot in English, about a Frenchman who needs an American signature — the layered foreignness is not decoration. The film is exact about what a person will sign in order to be allowed to remain somewhere, and about how much of a life gets built on top of the signature.

The warden wants the game played and he wants it lost, and the man he asks played professionally before he became an inmate. A prison football match between the guards and the men they guard means that for one afternoon the beatings are scored, and Robert Aldrich lets that condition sit for two hours before doing anything about it. The interest is not whether the deal gets taken. It is what a thrown game would cost men who have little left to trade but the way they carry themselves; self-esteem is the film's own word for it, and it is treated as a material resource, rationed by the institution. Aldrich shoots the football as labour: slow to organise, expensive to the body, settled by whoever keeps getting up. The comedy is not relief. In an American picture of 1974, aimed at an institution, humour is the only permitted form of contempt.

Samson killed Jamie, the rest of the group knows it, and not one of them can work out what a person is supposed to do next. Tim Hunter settles the crime early and spends the rest of the hundred minutes on conversation — who tells, who does not, what loyalty is owed and to whom — so the whole load is carried by how teenagers speak when they are frightened and refuse to be seen frightened. The Independent Spirit award its screenplay took is the useful marker here, more than the crime label on the shelf. Long passages go by in which nothing is decided, because deciding would mean admitting the size of the thing, and Hunter lets those passages stay as flat as they would be. It plays less like a thriller than a group portrait, taken at the point where friendship and complicity stop being distinguishable.

The wager is simple and not decent: get the Salvation Army missionary to Havana for a night. Two and a half hours of 1955 studio musical follow, and their shape is a collision between two ways of talking, one that prices everything as odds, one that refuses to price anything at all. The gambler's New York is a map of rooms, debts and figures carried in the head; the mission across from it counts souls and keeps its books in public. Joseph L. Mankiewicz lets neither vocabulary convert the other. They simply keep having to be used in the same room, which is what makes the romance work and what makes the songs feel less like interruptions than like the moment each side states its terms out loud. And underneath the trip there is a motive that has not been disclosed.
